summary: Specifies the DOTS data channel, used for bulk exchange of data that cannot easily or appropriately be sent over the signal channel during an attack. It is the companion to the DOTS signal channel in RFC 8782.

plainLanguage.summary: The alarm button needs a quick channel. For longer paperwork you use a calmer one. This is the paperwork channel.

subtitle: How a DDoS victim sends long-lived configuration, such as aliases and filtering rules, to its mitigation provider over RESTCONF.

tldr.problem: During a DDoS attack, the DOTS signal channel must stay small and robust, so it is a poor fit for bulk, infrequent data such as lists of prefixes and filtering rules.
tldr.mechanism: The DOTS data channel runs RESTCONF over TLS over TCP and defines a YANG module, 'ietf-dots-data-channel', that lets a DOTS client register itself, create aliases for protected resources, and install drop-list, accept-list and rate-limit rules on its DOTS server.
tldr.outcome: Clients get a reliable, authenticated way to manage aliases and filters ahead of and during an attack, with the signal channel referring to those aliases later. RFC 8783 is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8783 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the companion to the signal channel specification in RFC 8782.

sections.title: Two Channels for DDoS Defence
sections.content:
A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack tries to make machines or network resources unavailable to their intended users. DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) lets a DOTS client ask an upstream DOTS server for help. As RFC 8612 notes, the lack of a common method to coordinate a real-time response inhibits mitigation speed and effectiveness.

DOTS defines two channels. The signal channel (specified in RFC 8782) carries information about a device or network under attack. The data channel, specified here, is used for infrequent bulk data exchange that cannot easily or appropriately be sent over the signal channel under attack conditions.

The data channel does two main jobs: creating aliases for resources that may need mitigation, and policy management, meaning installing or withdrawing traffic filters, dropping or rate-limiting unwanted traffic, and permitting accept-listed traffic. A DOTS client may only instruct filtering rules on IP resources that belong to its own domain.
sections.plainLanguage: One channel is the fire alarm and the other is the filing cabinet. The alarm must always work. The filing cabinet holds the long lists you prepare so that help knows what to protect.

sections.title: Design of the Data Channel
sections.content:
Unlike the signal channel, the data channel is not expected to be fully operational at all times, especially during an attack. Because its main function is data exchange, it needs reliable transport so agents can tell whether delivery succeeded. The RFC therefore uses RESTCONF over TLS over TCP, with JSON payloads encoded as in RFC 7951.

The HTTP POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE methods edit data resources, and GET retrieves configuration and state. A client first discovers the RESTCONF API root and uses it as the start of every request path. The RFC does not require any order between creating the signal and data channels.

A client can keep a persistent connection or connect periodically. Clients SHOULD reuse the same TLS session, and MAY probe a quiet server with a TLS heartbeat to confirm it still holds TLS state. A server SHOULD support a configuration parameter that says what to do when two clients in one domain send conflicting rules, for example a drop-list and an accept-list entry for the same source prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of shouting, the client sends neat, signed letters through a reliable postal service, and gets a reply for each one saying whether it was accepted.

sections.title: Gateways, Loops and Stale Entries
sections.content:
A DOTS gateway can sit between client and server. When one is involved, it checks that the client is authorized, relays the request upstream, and passes the response back. The same rules for handling the client domain identifier cdid as in RFC 8782 apply, and the server checks that the gateway is authorized too.

To avoid infinite forwarding loops, gateways MUST support the procedure in Section 5.7.1 of RFC 7230. Each gateway MUST check that none of its own information is in the Via header field. If it is, the gateway MUST NOT forward the message, and a 508 Loop Detected status-line SHOULD be returned. Otherwise it appends its own information.

To avoid stale entries, every alias and filtering entry has a lifetime, and servers may also track client inactivity. Server discovery and how to choose among several servers are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter passes through a post office and sees its own stamp already on it, it knows it is going round in circles and stops. Old notes also get thrown away if nobody renews them.

sections.title: The YANG Data Model and Filters
sections.content:
The module ietf-dots-data-channel has a dots-client list keyed by cuid, with optional cdid, an aliases subtree and an acls subtree, plus read-only capabilities. Its ACLs mimic the structure of RFC 8519: an ordered list of ACLs, each holding an ordered list of access control entries (ACEs) with match and action criteria. ACLs are not bound to a device interface, and by default the destination of a rule is the DOTS client domain.

Actions are accept or drop, and accepted traffic can be rate-limited. There is deliberately no reject action, because sending ICMP errors during an attack would add load and tell the attacker that traffic is being blocked.

The module adds a fragment match for IPv4 and IPv6, and a TCP flags-bitmask match, because the existing flags field does not allow a bitmask. Implementations MUST support matching on IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP and ICMP headers. A client MUST NOT set fragment and flags (or flags-bitmask and flags) in the same request.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule is like a sticky note that says: if a packet looks like this, throw it away or let it in. There is no polite reply to the sender, because that would just help the bad guys.

sections.title: Registering Clients and Managing Aliases
sections.content:
A client MUST register by creating a dots-client resource, normally with a POST carrying its cuid, a globally unique client identifier. It MUST use the same cuid on the signal and data channels. A server-domain gateway SHOULD add cdid. A server returns 201 Created on success, 400 Bad Request if cuid is missing, and 409 Conflict if the resource exists. A client can deregister by deleting its resource, and the server then deletes everything bound to it.

An alias has a mandatory name and can list target-prefix, target-port-range, target-protocol, target-fqdn and target-uri. At least one of the prefix, FQDN or URI attributes MUST be present. Prefixes must not include broadcast, loopback or multicast addresses and must be within the client domain.

The RFC's example creates alias https1 for two IPv6 addresses on TCP port 443. A server MUST keep an alias for at least 10080 minutes (1 week) unless refreshed. GET retrieves one or all aliases, and a missing name gives 404 Not Found. DELETE returns 204 No Content.
sections.plainLanguage: First you sign in with your own ID. Then you can give nicknames to the things you want protected, like calling two web servers 'shop', so later you can just say 'protect the shop'.

sections.title: Managing Filtering Rules
sections.content:
A client MAY first GET the server's capabilities and SHOULD NOT request actions the server does not support. It then installs rules with POST or PUT. Each ACL has a name, an optional type, and an activation-type: activate-when-mitigating (the default), immediate or deactivate. Each ACE has matches and a mandatory actions entry. For immediate ACLs the destination prefix is mandatory, and servers MUST check that prefixes lie within the client's domain.

The first example blocks traffic from 192.0.2.0/24 to 198.51.100.0/24. Rate limits are in bytes per second, the same unit as traffic-rate in RFC 5575. A conflict with another client's rule gets 409 Conflict absent local policy, and a request via a gateway that the server has no cdid for gets 403 Forbidden, after which the client MUST register.

Rules are kept for at least 10080 minutes (1 week) unless refreshed, typically by a PUT that echoes a GET response without read-only parameters like pending-lifetime. Clients periodically query counters with GET, and DELETE removes a rule.
sections.plainLanguage: You write the rules on cards: block this crowd, let these friends in, or only let a few through per second. Cards expire after a while unless you renew them.

sections.title: Operations and Security
sections.content:
Operationally, a server MUST NOT enable both the data channel and direct configuration, to avoid races and inconsistent configuration. Agents SHOULD use the data channel for aliases and ACLs, keeping direct configuration only as a stop-gap for testing.

Agents MUST follow RESTCONF security guidance in RFC 8040 and support the mutual authentication TLS profile of RFC 8782. TLS with confidentiality protection is required and the guidance of RFC 7525 MUST be followed. TCP-AO can counter RST injection that would otherwise cause a denial of service on the connection.

Servers MUST verify that a client may only filter prefixes in its own domain. Rate-limiting requests, including those with new cuid values, and per-client quotas protect the server. The RFC also warns that an attacker with access to a client could set an arbitrarily low or high rate limit, or install invalid aliases and ACL entries.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the real owner of a house may ask for its doors to be locked, and the conversation is kept private. Otherwise a stranger could lock out your friends or let in the bad guys.
